title: Monotonic stack
summary: Keep a stack of positions whose answer is still unknown, in sorted order. A new item pops and answers every item it beats.
idea: Items waiting for a bigger value form a falling run. The next bigger value answers them from the top down, so each is popped once.

signals.see: For each item you need the next or previous item that is bigger or smaller.
signals.think: Keep indexes on a stack in sorted order. A new item pops every waiting item it beats and becomes their answer.

signals.see: You need a span: how many items in a row before this one were lower.
signals.think: Pop every lower item. The new top is the nearest higher item, and the span is the distance to it.

signals.see: The largest rectangle, or area, limited by the shortest bar in a range.
signals.think: Keep bars in rising order. When a shorter bar arrives, pop and measure the area each popped bar could reach.

signals.see: A nested loop that scans right from each item until it finds a bigger one.
signals.think: That is O(n²). One stack pass gives every answer in O(n).

phrasings: For each day's temperature, how many days until a warmer day?
For each building, find the first taller building to its right.
How many days in a row up to today had a share price no higher than today's?

picture.title: Answer the waiting items
picture.alt: On the left, each item scans right until it finds a bigger value, costing n times n steps. On the right, indexes wait on a stack in falling order and each new value pops every smaller waiting item, so each index is pushed and popped once.
picture.caption: Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the pass is linear.

before.label: Brute force: scan right from each

after.label: Pattern: pop what the new item beats

code.py:
def next_greater(nums):
    answer, stack = [-1] * len(nums), []  #@init
    for i in range(len(nums)):  #@loop
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[i]:  #@check
            answer[stack.pop()] = nums[i]  #@pop
        stack.append(i)  #@push
    return answer  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 12 whole numbers between -99 and 99, separated by commas.

oneLiner: for i: while top < nums[i] → pop and answer it; push i

exercise.prompt: prices[i] is a share price on day i. The span of day i is the number of days in a row, ending with day i, whose price was no higher than prices[i]. Return every span. The starter pushes each day but never pops, so it only works for falling prices. Add the pop loop.

starter.py:
def price_spans(prices):
    spans = []
    stack = []  # indexes of days with higher prices, nearest on top
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        # Pop every day whose price is not higher than prices[i].
        start = stack[-1] if stack else -1
        spans.append(i - start)
        stack.append(i)
    return spans

hints: A day with a price no higher than today can never be the stopping point for any later day either, so it can be popped for good.
Pop while the top price is <= prices[i]. Then the top, if any, is the nearest higher day, and the span is i minus its index.

complexity.why: The inner while loop looks nested, but every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work over the whole pass is at most 2n.

mistakes: Pushing values instead of indexes, so you cannot work out distances or fill the answer array.
Using < when the question needs <= (or the other way round). Decide what happens with equal values.
Calling the nested while loop O(n²). Each index is popped at most once, so it is O(n).
Forgetting the items left on the stack at the end: they have no answer, so keep their default.

quiz.question: Why is a monotonic stack pass O(n) even with a while loop inside the for loop?
choices: The while loop runs at most once
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once
The stack never holds more than 2 items
quiz.explain: Across the whole pass there are at most n pushes and n pops, so the total work is linear.

quiz.question: For next greater element, what order do the values on the stack keep from bottom to top?
quiz.explain: A bigger value pops everything smaller before it is pushed, so what remains is a falling run.

quiz.question: For stock spans, after popping all lower or equal prices, what does the top of the stack tell you?
choices: The nearest earlier day with a higher price
The first day of the list
quiz.explain: Everything lower was popped, so the top is the nearest higher day. The span is the distance to it, or i + 1 if the stack is empty.

interviewTip: State the invariant before coding: “the stack holds indexes still waiting for an answer, with falling values”. Then explain the O(n) cost as one push and one pop per index.
